comments.text: I don't understand the disconnect between people admitting they make bad financial decisions that lead to the inability to retire.  There is such a thing as getting too late to be able to retire.  Take it seriously, DON'T count on Social security providing the base of your retirement, DON'T expect the government to provide the majority of your finances in retirement, BECOME financially literate, be INTENTIONAL and DISCIPLINED for your working career.  Life is tough, wear a helmet.

comments.author: @collins4750
comments.text: I had a professor who taught a one-weekend seminar on finances and financial literacy and responsibility. It was one of the best courses i took. He showed diagrams of how retirement savings grow over time and that really stuck with me. the second I started my first "real" job out of school I made sure to start making max contributions for the employer match right out of the gate. I got used to not even having that 6% in my take home pay from the start. I still wonder how I would have approached saving for retirement had I not spent that one weekend in that seminar, learning all that I did. financial literacy NEEDS to be taught in school, and hopefully by an effective educator.

comments.text: I’m retiring in one week. I’m lucky that my employer offered me an amazing severance package, but I have very little saved (+/-10K). The only debt I have is my mortgage. I am four months from full retirement age according to Social Security, but I won’t be going that route until I am FRA plus six months in order to squeak every penny out of that SS check. I have figured that I can make it by living even more frugally as long as that mortgage payment doesn’t creep up even more.
